newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin faces tough task selling NATO deal at home.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces tough task selling NATO deal at home.

text.p: When Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov embraced Javier Solana after agreeing a breakthrough security deal with the NATO Secretary General on Wednesday, it was a sign of both joy and relief.
For Primakov and President Boris Yeltsin, the deal is not an outright victory but a consolation prize in a battle over NATO expansion which the Western defence alliance won hands down.

Yeltsin tried to make the best of a bad deal by trying to minimise the damage, winning as many concessions as possible and keeping relations with the West on track at the same time as criticising NATO expansion plans.

He now faces the tough task of selling the deal to a sceptical public and parliament. Criticism will be limited if he is seen to have won clear concessions, but he faces a fierce backlash if Russia is perceived to have gained nothing.

"It's a no-win situation for Yeltsin. If he doesn't sign the agreement, he faces criticism. If he does sign, he also comes under fire," said Sergei Karaganov, a foreign policy expert on Yeltsin's advisory Presidential Council.
"The administration was in a very difficult position. We have to wait to see the final document to see the details and judge what has been achieved."
The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation made clear from the start that it would expand with or without Russia's consent.
For Yeltsin, the overriding need was to try to convince Russians, and particularly his communist and nationalist foes, that he had done all he could to defend national interests.

He won agreement to create a joint NATO-Russia council and, in broader talks, boosted Russia's chances of joining such bodies as the Group of Seven industrial powers and the Paris Club of government creditors.
He sought written guarantees that NATO would not build up its forces or deploy nuclear weapons on the territory of new members and demanded a say in NATO decision-making.
The text of the document has not been released but it is unlikely that NATO bowed fully to those demands, making it unclear how the agreement will be received in Russia.
The document does not need formal approval of the communist-led State Duma, the lower house of parliament, but major opposition parties look certain to reject the deal.

That is likely to increase tension between the Kremlin and the Duma, which is already in conflict with the government over its plans to reduce spending and which can hold up economic legislation if it digs its heels in.

"It was a lose-lose situation politically -- a question of choosing the lesser of two evils and limiting the damage," said Dmtry Trenin, a political and defence analyst at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Moscow.
"The Duma is likely to reject any deal. This will cause political problems, but it has no formal meaning because Yeltsin does not need parliamentary approval for the agreement."
The initial reaction from communists was rejection. Liberal parliamentarians waited for details to comment fully.

Yeltsin, 66, is gambling on being able to handle a new conflict with the Duma. He has the power to dissolve it and call new elections if it gets out of hand, something the communists fear because they could lose their grip on the chamber.
He almost certainly calculated that he would have faced criticism from nationalists whatever he did.
Allowing NATO expansion to go ahead without an agreement tackling at least some of Moscow's concerns would have made him and Russian diplomacy look weak.

Russia might have excluded itself from talks on European security, provoked a freeze in relations with the West and risked pushing itself into isolation when it needs foreign assistance to help it through economic crisis.

Yeltsin may also have decided it was a question of a deal now or never -- NATO would have no obvious need to make concessions once the enlargement process begins when it offers invitations to new members at a Madrid summit in July.
"Yeltsin probably thought he had to solve this before Madrid, thinking he would gain nothing after it," said Alexei Pushkov, a member of the advisory Foreign and Defence Policy Council.

Looking ahead to a G7 summit in Denver which Yeltsin is to attend in June, he said: "He also wants to go to Denver on good terms with (U.S. President Bill) Clinton, (German Chancellor Helmut) Kohl and the others."
